issues.legal_issue: An endowment established for a deity and administered by family members as managers is a public religious and charitable trust when the evidence shows that the family held no beneficial ownership.
material_facts: An agreement made by the family stated that the villages had been granted for worship of the deity, that the temple belonged to the deity’s institution, and that no family member had a share in it.
A later family agreement described family maintenance payments as remuneration for service to the deity.
The Inam Commissioner recorded the villages as permanent religious endowments after the family representative challenged their recording as personal grants.

Family members and the appellant repeatedly described the deity as owner and themselves as managers; the appellant’s published history likewise said the institution was not private or family property.
The original grant documents that the appellant relied on were not produced, and the documents produced did not contradict the admissions or revenue records.
issues.conclusion: The temple and its properties constituted a public religious and charitable endowment, and the appellant had not established private ownership.
issues.legal_principle: The nature of an endowment is determined from the evidence as a whole, including the terms and history of grants, admissions, records, and administration. Under the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, section 5(3), the suit concerned the character of the alleged trust. Srinivasa Chariar v. Evalappa Mudaliar (1922) applied the principle that where the origins show property to be trust property, the trustee bears a heavy onus to establish personal acquisition by clear and unimpeachable evidence. Arunachalam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guru Swamigal (1919) recognized the weight of official inam records. The court distinguished Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop (1939), where the grant was made to an individual and his heirs.

rule.if: suit_challenging_endowment and family_admitted_deity_ownership and official_records_show_endowment and original_grant_evidence_not_produced

predicates.suit_challenging_endowment: A claimant brought a suit disputing whether property associated with a religious institution was held as an endowment.
predicates.family_admitted_deity_ownership: Members of the managing family stated that the deity owned the institution or its property and that the family acted as managers or servants.
predicates.official_records_show_endowment: Official records identified the property as held for the religious institution or deity.
predicates.original_grant_evidence_not_produced: The claimant did not produce the original grant evidence relied on to support private ownership.

issues.definition: When an endowment is challenged, family admissions and official records showing ownership by the deity, combined with failure to produce the original grant evidence, support finding a public religious endowment.

issues.legal_issue: Longstanding public worship as of right, considered with the character and use of a temple, supports the inference that the temple is public.
material_facts: The public had worshipped at the temple for more than 200 years, and there was no evidence that the public had been excluded.
The temple was extensive, included a large assembly hall, and admitted worshippers throughout the day.
Public festivals, processions, ceremonies, offerings, and feeding were conducted at the temple.
Rulers had granted land and money for worship and festivals.
The idol was sometimes moved temporarily for processions or visits, and a substitute was left for worship at the temple.
issues.conclusion: The temple and deity were public, and the public had a right of worship; temporary movement of the idol did not make the temple private.
issues.legal_principle: In Narayanan v. Hindu Religious Endowments Board, A.I.R. 1938 Mad. 209, the court treated long public user, a separate endowment, the institution’s character and administration, and the absence of arbitrary exclusion as grounds for inferring public dedication and public use as of right. The court also considered Ram Soondur Thakoor v. Taruk Chunder Turkoruttum (1873), Hari Raghunath v. Anantji Bhikaji (1920), Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (1925), and Venkatachala v. Sambasiva, A.I.R. 1927 Mad. 465. It held that temporary movement of an idol, the absence of a dome or kalas, and the lack of consecration for a swayambhu deity were not by themselves decisive against public character.

rule.if: public_worship_longstanding and no_evidence_of_public_exclusion and temple_has_public_character and public_endowment_or_grants

predicates.public_worship_longstanding: Members of the public worshipped at the institution over a long period.
predicates.no_evidence_of_public_exclusion: The evidence did not show that the institution’s managers excluded members of the public from worship.
predicates.temple_has_public_character: The institution’s scale, layout, ceremonies, or administration were characteristic of a place used for public worship.
predicates.public_endowment_or_grants: The institution received grants or endowments for worship, festivals, or related religious purposes.

issues.definition: Longstanding public worship without evidence of exclusion, together with public features of the institution and religious endowments, supports a finding that the public has a right of worship.

issues.legal_issue: A party relying on admissions against its claim must displace them with cogent evidence, while the abstract burden of proof is immaterial when both sides have adduced evidence that can be weighed.
material_facts: The appellant and his predecessors had repeatedly admitted that the public could worship at the temple and that the properties were held for the deity.
The appellant did not establish that those admissions were erroneous or unavailable against him.
Both sides introduced evidence on the character of the deity and properties, which the courts weighed.
issues.conclusion: The appellant had to prove that the admissions were erroneous or did not bind him, and he failed to do so; the abstract allocation of the burden of proof was academic once the evidence had been led.
issues.legal_principle: An admission is strong evidence for the opposing party and, although not conclusive, may decide the matter unless successfully withdrawn or shown to be erroneous. “Burden of proof” may mean either the obligation to prove an allegation to obtain judgment or the obligation to introduce evidence on a contested issue. The latter allocation becomes academic where both parties have adduced evidence and the court can weigh it. The court applied Srinivasa Chariar v. Evalappa Mudaliar (1922) to the burden on a trustee claiming personal acquisition of property shown to have trust origins.

rule.if: contested_property_claim and both_sides_led_evidence and claimant_or_predecessors_made_admissions and admissions_not_displaced

predicates.contested_property_claim: A claimant disputed whether property was held for a religious institution or privately.
predicates.both_sides_led_evidence: Each side introduced evidence on the disputed character of the property.
predicates.claimant_or_predecessors_made_admissions: The claimant or predecessors in title made statements inconsistent with the claimant’s present position.
predicates.admissions_not_displaced: The claimant did not prove that the statements were erroneous, withdrawn, or unavailable as evidence.

issues.definition: When both sides have produced evidence, unrebutted admissions by the claimant or predecessors support the opposing claim rather than making the abstract burden allocation decisive.

issues.legal_issue: Official inam-register entries carry great weight in determining the history and nature of property when no authentic contrary evidence is available.
material_facts: The Inam Commissioner investigated the villages and recorded them as permanent religious endowments after the family representative appealed the initial personal-inam classification.
The appellant did not produce the earlier sanads referred to in the official records and history of the institution.
The later documents produced by the appellant did not contradict the official records or the admissions concerning the endowment.
issues.conclusion: The Inam Register entries were entitled to great weight and prevailed in the absence of authentic contrary evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Arunachalam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guru Swamigal (1919) held that inam-register material reflects official inquiry and is important evidence of a property’s history and tenure. It does not displace actual and authentic evidence in an individual case, but prevails where such evidence is absent.

predicates.civil_property_dispute: A civil proceeding required the court to determine the nature or tenure of property.
predicates.official_register_based_on_inquiry: An official register recorded the property after an investigation into its title or tenure.
predicates.no_authentic_contrary_evidence: No authentic individual evidence contradicting the official entry was produced.

issues.definition: In a civil property dispute, an official entry based on inquiry prevails when no authentic evidence contradicts it.

issues.legal_issue: A concurrent inference drawn from documents is a finding of fact where the documents have not been misconstrued.
material_facts: The two lower courts examined the documentary evidence and reached concurrent conclusions about the public endowment.
The appellant challenged the inferences drawn from the documents but did not establish that the documents had been misconstrued.
The original grant documents that could have supported the appellant’s account were not produced.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings were findings of fact and could not be overturned on the asserted ground that the inferences from the documents were mistaken.
issues.legal_principle: A mistaken inference from documents remains a finding of fact if the documents themselves have not been misconstrued. The Supreme Court could not reopen the concurrent findings on the appellant’s argument without established misconstruction.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter came before the court as an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.concurrent_findings_based_on_documents: The lower courts reached the same factual conclusion after considering documentary evidence.
predicates.document_misconstruction_not_established: The appellant did not establish that the lower courts had misconstrued the documents.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, concurrent factual findings based on documents remain undisturbed when misconstruction of those documents is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking a declaration that property belongs privately to the claimant cannot effectively determine the deity’s interests if the deity is not joined as a party, and joining representatives of the public does not cure that omission.
material_facts: The appellant sought declarations that the deity and properties were private and opposed the respondents’ request to join the deity through an independent representative.
Representatives of the Hindu public were later joined under the representative-suit procedure, but the deity remained absent.
The trial judge had warned that the suit could be dismissed if the deity proved to be a necessary party.
The appellant sought to add the deity only at a late stage of the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The omission of the deity could not be cured by joining representatives of the public, and no effective declaration binding the deity could be made in its absence.
issues.legal_principle: A suit affecting the interests of a deity must include the deity as a party so that an effective and binding decree can be made. Joining public representatives under Order 1, rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not substitute for the deity. The court referred to Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (1925) and Kanhaiya Lal v. Hamid Ali (1933) in declining to permit a late procedural course in light of the appellant’s opposition and the warning given below.

predicates.declaratory_suit_affecting_deity_interes: A claimant sought a declaration about property or rights that would affect a deity’s interests.
predicates.deity_not_joined: The deity was not made a party to the suit.
predicates.public_representatives_joined: Representatives of the worshipping public were joined in the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a declaration affects a deity’s interests, joining public representatives without joining the deity does not permit an effective decree against the deity.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding whether property is a public religious trust need not determine individual rights to worship, management, or maintenance that are outside the trust-character issue.
material_facts: The trial judge also made findings about the customary worship, management, and maintenance rights of individual defendants.
The suit was brought to determine whether the properties were held as a public religious and charitable trust.
The Supreme Court dismissed the suit as a whole and declined to give directions on those individual rights.
issues.conclusion: The individual rights findings were not necessary to determine the trust’s public character and should not have been decided in this suit.
issues.legal_principle: In a suit under section 5(3) of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, the issue to be determined was whether the property constituted a trust of a public nature; the court considered individual rights to be outside that issue.

predicates.suit_to_determine_public_trust_character: The proceeding was brought to determine whether property was held as a public trust.
predicates.court_decides_individual_worship_or_mana: The court was asked to determine or made findings on particular persons’ rights to worship, manage, or receive maintenance.

issues.definition: A proceeding limited to determining public-trust character does not determine individual worship, management, or maintenance rights.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent cannot obtain a change to a costs order in an appeal without challenging that order by cross-objection.
material_facts: The trial court awarded two sets of costs, and the High Court modified the award to one set.
The respondents who sought further relief on costs did not file a cross-objection to the High Court’s decision.
issues.conclusion: No further relief on costs could be granted to those respondents because they had not filed a cross-objection.
issues.legal_principle: The court declined to vary the High Court’s costs decision in the absence of a cross-objection by the respondents seeking that relief.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter came before the court as an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.respondent_seeks_costs_variation: A respondent asked the appellate court to alter the costs order in the respondent’s favour.
predicates.no_cross_objection: The respondent did not file a cross-objection challenging the costs decision.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a respondent seeking alteration of a costs order receives no such relief when the respondent has filed no cross-objection.
